title: TikTok Is Turning Karol G’s Album Release Into a Live Fan Event - WeRSM
content: TikTok is making Karol G’s album release a live appointment. On November 4, the Colombian artist will perform songs from No Me Arrepiento De Sentir Tanto in a one-hour TikTok LIVE Premiere, streamed from 8:00 to 9:00 PM Mexico City time. The event will run on Karol G’s official TikTok account, giving her audience a shared moment around an album that has already reached No. 1 on Billboard’s Top Latin Albums chart. The platform’s official announcement positions the livestream as more than a concert broadcast. It is a way to connect a major music release directly to the fan behavior TikTok has helped create. Karol G has more than 56 million followers on TikTok, while “Si Antes Te Hubiera Conocido” has appeared in more than 1.7 million user-created videos. That gives TikTok something most music platforms cannot easily replicate: a visible, active layer of participation around the artist and her songs. The livestream brings that participation into the release moment itself. Fans in Medellín and Madrid can watch the same performance at the same time, with comments running alongside the set. The audience is not only consuming the album. It is reacting publicly and collectively as the artist performs it. TikTok has already tested this broader release playbook with Karol G. Around her 2025 album Tropicoqueta, the platform created an AI Karol G effect, themed profile frames, and a leaderboard ranking countries by views of related content. LIVE Premiere adds a real-time layer to that existing system of effects, posts, fandom signals, and discovery. That matters because TikTok is moving closer to the center of the music launch, not simply serving as the place where songs become popular after release. With LIVE Premiere, the platform can help shape the moment itself, then let fans extend it through comments, clips, reactions, and new videos. For artists, the value is a tighter connection between attention and participation. For TikTok, it is another reason for fans to stay inside the app when a cultural moment is happening. The album remains the product, but the live community response becomes part of the release strategy.

China’s Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT) has leaked the official product images and filing data for the upcoming Buick Electra GS plug-in hybrid sedan. Developed by the SAIC-GM joint venture, the large, fastback-style sedan is tailored specifically for the Chinese market and is very unlikely to ever set wheels on American land due to regulatory hurdles and prohibitive tariffs. The production version represents a significant departure from the much taller, hatchback-like Electra GS Concept that made its debut in April 2025 as a preview of a future production model. And this is it! It may not be the concept car’s identical twin, but it is the next best thing. With styling that pays tribute to Buick’s iconic Gran Sport lineup, the Electra GS PHEV car features ultra-slim, C-shaped LED headlights linked by an LED strip. The Buick tri-shield logo sits right below on a less aggressive "shark-nose" front fascia. The Electra GS is the slightly shorter and potentially more affordable alternative to Buick’s existing Electra L7 Sportback sedan. It measures 190.0 inches (4,980 millimeters) in length, 75.4 inches (1,915 millimeters) in width, and 58.9 inches (1,495 millimeters) in height, sitting on a wheelbase of 112.8 inches (2,865 millimeters). Those numbers make it slightly smaller than the Buick Electra L7. The leaked documents confirm the plug-in hybrid setup, which combines the electric motor, good for 221 horsepower (224 metric horsepower), with either the naturally aspirated 1.5-liter or the turbocharged 1.5-liter inline-four. The naturally aspirated engine produces 72 horsepower (73 metric horsepower, while the turbocharged unit churns out 154 horsepower (156 metric horsepower). The base variant rolls off the production line with 318 horsepower (322 metric horsepower), while the range-topping turbocharged example sees the light of day with a combined system output of 375 horsepower (380 metric horsepower). GM hasn’t revealed any pricing details either, but it will most likely happen closer to the launch date set for early 2027. While the Buick Electra GS PHEV will stay away from the U.S., it has every chance to make it to the European market. title: The Lexus GS America Never Got: This Twin-Turbo 2JZ Toyota Aristo V300 Is Live at No Reserve - Yahoo Autos
content: Americans who wanted a Lexus GS 300 got a naturally aspirated inline-six. Japan got the twin-turbo version. This 1998 Toyota Aristo V300 is live at no reserve on Cars & Bids with a twin-turbocharged 2JZ, right-hand drive and a U.S. title, and the auction ends Friday, November 6 at 1:42 PM EST. At the time of writing, the high bid was $9,000 with 11 bids. Toyota launched the second-generation Aristo in Japan in 1997. According to the listing, it was closely related to the Lexus GS sold in the United States, and Japanese buyers could choose between two versions of the 2JZ engine in a rear-wheel-drive chassis. The U.S. GS 300 got the naturally aspirated 3.0-liter six, rated at 225 horsepower. The Aristo V300 added a pair of turbochargers, and the listing puts output at about 276 horsepower and 333 lb-ft of torque, sent to the rear wheels through a four-speed automatic. That is roughly 50 more horsepower than the American car. The package is a quiet luxury sedan with leather, a power sunroof and navigation, built around the same engine family that made the Supra famous. The Aristo nameplate was retired in 2005. This silver Aristo has a black interior and shows approximately 113,300 kilometers on its metric odometer, or about 70,400 miles, according to the seller. It is titled in Montana and located in North Highlands, California. The seller lists leather upholstery, heated front seats, automatic dual-zone climate control, navigation, cruise control and traction control, along with a power sunroof and rear sunshade. Modifications reported by the seller are modest: Bilstein coilovers, 18-inch BBS LM wheels, a TRD exhaust system, a Team Toyota Europe front lip spoiler, and a Japanese ETC toll unit. A recent compression test is posted in the photo gallery, and the listing includes a cold-start video, a walkaround and an air-conditioning vent temperature test. The seller discloses chips, scratches and scuffs on the nose, weathered and scratched wheels, creases on the driver's seat, and corrosion on some engine bay and underbody components. The seller reports buying the car in 2026 and adding about 500 miles since. The car is titled to the seller's LLC, and only one key is included. As with any imported car, registration is the buyer's responsibility. The seller notes that the Aristo may not pass emissions testing in some states, so check local rules before placing a bid. Twin-turbo 2JZ cars are not usually cheap. A 1997 Supra Turbo 15th Anniversary Edition bid past $52,000 on Cars & Bids earlier this year. The Aristo shares an engine family with that car and adds four doors and a back seat. It also fits the growing market for Japanese-market sedans and wagons, as shown when a right-hand-drive 1998 Toyota Caldina wagon sold for $7,700. The Aristo has the sort of drivetrain tuners have chased for decades, wrapped in a body that rarely draws a second glance. With no reserve, it will sell to the highest bidder on Friday afternoon. title: Buick Doesn’t Sell Sedans in the U.S., But China Will Get the Sleek New Electra GS Plug-In Hybrid - Car and Driver
content: Designed for the Chinese market, the Electra GS looks significantly different than the concept shown last year, with sharp, C-shaped LED headlights. While there are reports of a new sedan on the horizon, Buick’s lineup in the United States currently only consists of SUVs. But over in China, Buick offers a healthy arsenal of sedans, from the compact Verano to the larger LaCrosse. Now Buick is about to introduce a new electrified sedan called the Electra GS, and the first images of the new car have been leaked via China’s Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT). The MIIT periodically publishes information on upcoming automotive products, and the official filing is the first time we’ve seen the final production design for the Electra GS, which was first previewed by a concept in 2025. Confusingly, Buick already offers a sedan called the Electra L7 in China, sold with electric and range-extender plug-in hybrid powertrains, but the new Electra GS seems poised to be a less potent and more affordable option. The new Electra GS is a bit smaller than the Electra L7, measuring 196.0 inches from nose to tail, just over two inches shy of the L7. The GS is also 1.5 inches narrower and has a 5.3-inch shorter wheelbase than the L7. Under the hood, the Electra GS will employ a plug-in hybrid setup that uses either a 97-hp naturally aspirated 1.5-liter inline-four or a turbocharged 1.5-liter making 154 hp. The gas engines are paired with an electric motor producing 221 horsepower, which feeds off a lithium iron phosphate battery. Stylistically, the production Electra GS is a significant departure from the concept, with a more traditional sedan shape than the concept’s taller, hatchback look. The front end has thin headlights that wrap around a trim piece that stretches across the front and can be either body colored or finished in silver. The Electra GS has a fastback roofline and smooth surfacing, while the taillights span the width of the vehicle before curving inward. Overall, the Electra GS looks smart and modern, and Buick will hope that the GS can help reverse its sales slide in China. The Electra GS won’t be coming to the U.S., but it could give a sense of Buick’s future styling direction that could appear on the rumored gas-powered sedan expected to arrive in the next couple of years. Aaru, a two-and-a-half-year-old startup valued at $1 billion, is redefining market research and consumer intelligence by deploying multi-agent AI simulations to predict how humans will make decisions. Cam Fink, co-founder and CEO, and Ned Koh, co-founder and president, discuss Aaru's founding story and how advanced behavioral simulation overcomes the limitations of traditional consumer polling. In this conversation with Goldman Sachs Chief Information Officer Marco Argenti, they also explore the real-world enterprise applications of such predictive simulations across retail, financial services, and utilities, which are driving Aaru's rapid rise. Cam Fink:    We help you understand the composition of any population on the globe, and what decisions they make. What marketing campaigns they're going to click on, what subway lines they're going to ride. Ned Koh:      Our model is able to process how humans are able to think. Marco Argenti:      Welcome to Talks at GS. And also welcome to Ned and Cam from Aaru. Nowadays with AI almost like anything is possible, including being 19 and then, you know, having a $1 billion valuation startup, which is pretty incredible. So, since then, Aaru has become one of the most closely watched companies in the research and intelligence space. Thank you for being here. Cam Fink:    Thank you, Marco, for hosting us. We're really glad to have the opportunity today to talk a bit more about what we do. Marco Argenti:      The first question I'm going to ask you is, when was the first time you kind of realized that AI was something big? Cam Fink:    So, it's interesting you ask this because the ChatGPT moment was right in our senior year of high school. So, I remember, you know, having worked in the NLP space, in the computer vision space, where Ned and I were researchers before ChatGPT was released. You could tell that like AI was gaining a lot of capabilities very quickly. But it wasn't until it became actually productized into something consumers could use that all of a sudden it felt like not only was AI going to gain capabilities, but actually that it would create serious change in how people work on, you know, ideas, on products. But even still, like I remember the most enterprising students were already using AI to evaluate their answers to papers or come up with new ideas or test new things. And if you were even more enterprising before that, you would have been using the GPT-3 API to try and finish papers. So, you know, I think that was truly the moment that it became clear AI was going to be inevitable. Marco Argenti:      Was there another ah-ha moment recently? Because, you know, right now it feels like things are changing so fast. What's another inflection point that you've seen? Ned Koh:      The tools are incredibly powerful for being used for incredibly rudimentary application: note taking, you know, or summarization as like the key use cases or demonstrations of like how this can help you. And I still think in many businesses it is. It's easy to get behind. There's not really any friction to adopting those technologies. And so, I think that the larger change is this wave of product-first AI businesses. You saw that in health care. You saw that in, you know, financial services and beyond. But I think it was when it went beyond just those into more complex applications, for sure. Marco Argenti:      So, rolling back, like, kind of two basics. If you're in front of a CEO that doesn't know what Aaru is and you have a few seconds to explain, what would you say to them? What's your pitch? Like you're 30 second pitch. Cam Fink:    We predict human behavior. So, we help you understand the composition of any population on the globe and what decisions they make. We can help you understand how U.S. household purchase decision makers are going to purchase products, what marketing campaigns they're going to click on, what music they're going to stream, what subway lines they're going to ride. That's really the core of what we do: predicting behavior to make better business decisions. Marco Argenti:      And I think we met maybe two years ago for the first time. So, really early on. So, what have you learned in terms of sort of what kinds of decisions is AI really good at predicting and what others are not that good? Ned Koh:      Yeah, I think the first place that you look when you define what good means is understanding like the relative for how people make those decisions today. Right? So, let's take something that's like very simple - product launches. So, you have someone who's going in front of a survey, you're asking people questions. It's easy to benchmark. And that's a very interesting market. Product innovation is massive for us. But when you think about like use cases and how that's kind of diverged across the board, the most relevant ones for us and where we offer the most amount of value, of course, are places where you may not traditionally have data. Right? And so, that may exist in a population who doesn't respond to surveys. The example I like to give is like everybody in this room is wearing a shirt. Did anyone tell someone how much they were willing to pay for it? Probably not. Right? But then you get into like other categories. Right. You know this answer better than I do. But you know, there are four industries that make up about like 15% of the GDP of the U.S. Airlines, telecom, utilities, insurance. What are the times that matter to those companies about their behavior? When do you remember who your cell provider is? When your cell service goes out. When do you remember that you pay bills to Con Ed? When your power goes out. When do you remember that you fly a specific airline versus another? When your flight gets delayed. Right? And so, on and so forth. When do you remember who your insurance is? When you crash a car. And so, those businesses, despite being massive, the most important place and time for them to understand the behavior of their customers is somewhere where it's fundamentally impossible to get inside their head inside that moment. Right? And so, the most interesting use cases to us have always been those areas that have the most challenging to reach groups. The time frames of traditional research, it can take weeks and weeks or months to get people in a room and ask them questions or show them a product. You don't have the ability to do that. Right? So, things that are compressed in timeline are the use cases that are most relevant for simulation because human insight just doesn't reach that same level. Marco Argenti:      But why can't you just ask ChatGPT? Cam Fink:    Language models themselves alone can't understand human behavior with the depth and the capability that is required to actually allow a business to trust their decisions. There are a lot of startups out there now doing what you might call synthetic personas. That's sort of like the last generation of the technology we build. They can be useful. Those startups can help you get like a really quick read on marketing copy. But if you want a decision that you can trust, you need something that's grounded in real world outcomes. And that's where someone like Aaru would come in. Everything we do is AI. Right? So, what underpins our capabilities to predict human behavior are models. Models that we train. Models that leverage LLMs but aren't LLMs alone. But through fusing kind of LLMs with statistical models and traditional mathematical models, we're able to be far more accurate and take advantage of all of LLMs’ advantages without falling into those kind of gaps with LLMs and predicting behavior. Marco Argenti:      And how do you verify the accuracy and the results? I mean, what is what's ground truth for you guys? Ned Koh:      At the end of the day, if you're trying to predict and make a decision better, what you should be aiming for is a better business outcome. That was very first principle to us, right? You want to benchmark it to the sales result, to the product selling better or selling worse or the limited time offer not flying off the shelves like you wanted it to. The way that we've been able to grow our business so quickly is by making sure that people walk out of a pilot with us and don't just say, "Yes, we came to a decision faster," but rather we came to a decision better than we otherwise would have. Marco Argenti:      So, let's actually kind of bring it to life a little bit with some examples. What does the client actually get? Give us some examples of that. Cam Fink:    So, we do a lot of work with CPG companies. We do a lot of work with retail, beauty, apparel, kind of like anything that touches a consumer brand. And every kind of business ultimately sells a product. But for consumer brands, it's typically really linear. You can hold the product in your hand, right? A canned beverage, a carton of milk, whatever it might be. So, we do a lot of product innovation work where we'll go work with, you know, a canned sparkling water company, for example. And that sparkling water company will come to us and say, "Hey, we've built this great business around this one core product. What is our next new product line, right? Is it still hydration? Is it a shelf-stable dairy product? Is it an energy drink? Is it--," you know, all of these things. And we can use Aaru to do everything from the very core conceptual stage of what is the next frontier, right, all the way into figuring out who exactly is the purchasing audience. Then into the product concept itself specifically. So, say we pick out that it's an energy drink. We figure out who the energy drink purchaser is going to be from this brand. And then we figure out, okay, what flavors of energy drink do we want to put out in the world? And then we can do everything from getting as niche as optimizing the caffeine content to helping figure out the right pack size and carry that entire product innovation cycle from start to finish in just a few weeks. And one of our clients we worked with, their product innovation cycle traditionally was nine months long, right? That's actually pretty quick for the CPG industry. A lot of the big global companies might be taking 12 months, 18 months, to go from product idea or, you know, new market entrant to ready for manufacturing. We managed to squeeze it down into eight weeks. That was a really, really, really powerful case study. And now the product ended up hitting the shelves earlier this year. And they saw more success than they had with any of their previous product launches before. Marco Argenti:      And if I remember, that you guys can decide the size of the core. Tell us a little bit about that spectrum. Cam Fink:    Yeah, we don't go down to individual-by-individual level, right? We're never processing PII or any kind of individual data. So, we can't recreate Tom Smith from Iowa or Cameron Fink from New York City, right? We can get down to audiences that in the real world might only be a couple hundred people. I remember at one point doing hospitals that have to purchase this third-party risk management software. You're probably talking only a few hundred to low thousands of people nationwide. And yet we were still able to recreate that audience. And for the company that we did do that study for, they saw a massive impact from the work we could do together. So, we're getting really niche. We can talk about very small groups of buyers or social media influencers or Gen Z in one particular city metro. And then we can go as wide as US household purchase decision-makers or British residents or, you know, even residents of the EU if you want it. Marco Argenti:      And where do you get your data? Cam Fink:    I mean, it's a massive wealth of data sources, right? So, when we talk about how we leverage that data, we have audience data and we have behavioral outcomes data. On the audience data component, that's what helps us understand who actually exists inside of a population. So, when you come to me and you say, "Hey, I want to talk to ultra high net worth individuals in, you know, the United States and Canada," we can actually tell you what the distribution of that population looks like. And then we have behavioral outcome data. That helps us figure out what decisions are they going to make. So, that would, you know, be for each of these given value propositions, how will UHMW individuals react to them? Now, when it comes to where that data actually comes from, you can think about three different buckets for each of the data sources that we leverage. The first would be publicly accessible data. We're leveraging tons of things like the census, academic research where there's license to train on top of it, you know, anything else available publicly that our model is able to use. Then there's a lot of data we purchase. So, we buy data from everyone from credit card, you know, purchase history data providers to receipts, there are music streams, social media data. And then I would say really the final component is proprietary partnerships that we leverage. So, we do a lot of work with organizations that wouldn't fit the shape of traditional customers of ours but still want access to the impact of our software. We have done data sharing through those sorts of engagements before that's been incredibly powerful for what we do too. Marco Argenti:      How do you make your clients comfortable that they can share their most valuable data? Cam Fink:    Every client is sandboxed entirely. We're SOC 2 compliant. I didn't expect that I'd be saying that up on stage. But just in case anyone was worried, we have any InfoSec people in the room, we are SOC 2 compliant. We have all the compliance certifications we can. Most importantly, we do not train on customer data. And all of our clients are sandboxed. So, we actually end up being trusted as one of the most secure places to store, you know, that data because you would never be able to leverage a traditional research provider for anything sensitive. Right? You wouldn't want to go survey people and then someone takes a screenshot and says, "Hey, you know, my favorite brand was polling me about this on the internet." Instead, when you're leveraging our software, it's kept entirely secure to, you know, the model that we train. Marco Argenti:      You just said the models that we train. So, has your attitude and approach shifted over the years with regards to kind of using your own models versus using frontier models versus using quasi frontier open-source models? Cam Fink:    Yeah, our approach has definitely changed. I mean, when we started the business, we were definitely more in this realm of like, hey, can you take an LLM and train it on top of survey results? We found some of our own issues with that, right? Historically, we found it wasn't extensible. And that's what really led us to the next generation of our technology. So, those are all the models that we built ourselves. And that was really the big leap forward in terms of how our technology was able to reach the accuracy level that it is today. And so, we've been on, you know, all of our own models ever since that point in time. LLMs help us write analysis. They help us do tons of tasks as part of the simulation pipeline. But LLMs aren't driving the fundamental underlying prediction and behavior themselves. Now, when it comes to the LLMs we integrate, we use tons of different providers. We default to whatever is the best provider for each task that we have to do. Marco Argenti:      Which could be, you know, somehow maybe filtering all the data or explaining or prompt interpretation. But then the actual prediction machine or the simulation machine is your own. And that's your secret sauce. Ned Koh:      That is the secret sauce. Every single economist in the history of like behavioral science and everything else that you can go into has dreamed to be able to build a model off of something that's based on outcomes. You want to be able to remove as much bias as possible. Right? And so, not always is the magic and the data exclusively. It's much more in how our model is able to process things that are in many ways useless by their own right into something that can become a holistic view of how humans are able to think. Marco Argenti:      If every customer is protected and everything, how do you evolve the model? Cam Fink:    We're integrating new data sources all the time, right? So, the data that we have alone is enough that we are able to go out and make tons of valuable predictions. We can generate a lot of insight without having to integrate client data. Integrating client data for us is the key to unlock, you know, much deeper capabilities and integrations, both in terms of, you know, the simulation component and also in terms of how simulation results end up getting used. Marco Argenti:      I get that. But within, let's say, client engagement though, let's say we use it in private wealth in GS and then we want to kind of continue to learn, so do you allow your clients to continuously learn on the model that you provide and that stays theirs? Cam Fink:    It's actually interesting. A huge part of what we're talking about now is this idea of compounding intelligence. One of the biggest issues that our clients feel, one of their biggest pains, is this idea that traditional insight is very static, right? You run one survey, you run another survey, maybe you run a quarterly brand tracker, but it's not like those survey results are propelling forth the next survey that you run. And when you think about simulation, what's really incredible about the difference with our platform is that it's not just the power to like access more accurate, faster results. Our simulations can also contain the insights from all the simulations before it. And what that means is that it actually builds and compounds in value over time. You can imagine someone using our platform at the end of running nine projects about studying the Gen Z audience together, could come to us and say, "What are the insights, you know, we didn't even know we had about the Gen Z audience?" And that can go into helping build the next product that people might be interested in. So, a big focus for us is that compounding intelligence piece. Marco Argenti:      Are you guys mostly focused on the US, or do you have a lot of international customers? Cam Fink:    Yeah, we're a totally global business in terms of what we support. So, when you think about the range of Aaru today, it's over 130 countries across the globe. All of the EU, all of North America, much of South Asia, Southeast Asia, you know, and beyond. In the future, we are actually planning international expansion starting soon. But today, the bulk of our customers are based in North America. Marco Argenti:      And so, on that note, so do you think you need to tune sort of your models by culture and by countries? Ned Koh:      I think one of the best markets that is super relevant for a lot of the biggest enterprises that we work with today is expansion into Germany is really interesting, right? I've seen this across customers of ours in consumer electronics. I've seen this across customers of ours in financial services, right? Like it really goes across so many areas. The amount of safety regulations that people care about in like South Florida versus in, you know, Central Germany are vastly different. I can tell you that, right? Like the reality is, you know, you talk about why do we train models within this time when you're actually in runtime? Why do we keep them updated? These sorts of elements. The news, the way they digest social media, the things that changed their environment is what we like to call it within a given sim. Absolutely do. The context of how you and I make decisions on today versus tomorrow, absolutely do change. Does my race change? No, that's not the most important part to measure. So, we absolutely have to do that and have to do it on a hyper localized basis. Marco Argenti:      What's your biggest bottleneck at this point? Cam Fink:    100% hiring. Like it's the best people in the world is the number one thing you need for any fast-growing business. And so, when we think about what is going to-- has defined the last six months, going to define the next six months, next six years of Aaru, it's all going to be about working with the best people in the world. Marco Argenti:      And what kind of people are you looking for? Cam Fink: The first thing that we evaluate for is raw capability. We do look for people who are the best in the world at something. Right? People who are truly excellent at the craft or at their craft, so to speak, and represent the pinnacle of understanding knowledge capability in a given area. That's something that every person wants. Right? I'm sure Goldman wants people who are the best in their craft as well. We also look for people who are really high slope. So, even if you're not the absolute best in the world at something today, do you have the potential to be that in the future? Can you learn quickly? Can you adapt is something that's really important to us as well. And then finally, we look for people who are real collaborators. Every time someone joins our team, it's not just about whether or not they themselves are a really, really brilliant individual. Tons of people who are super smart and, you know, would be lucky to work at any incredible business on the globe. We spend a lot of time focusing on who is exactly right for Aaru and the people who have much to teach our team, much to teach myself, but we also have much to teach them and they can be, you know, leverage, exponential or multiplicative leverage to the people around them. Ned Koh:      Most of our research team, right, you'll have people who are pure math backgrounds. You'll have people who have done Alzheimer's and dementia research, right, who are able to tie in these really interesting areas. On the other side, we've recently brought on the head of research and data science from Qualtrics, who was there for over 13 years. Right? It's like you need some of those incredibly experienced perspectives to understand how to solve these problems. But you also need very fresh ones to think outside of the box to be able to do it as well. It's all about a combination and a balance. Cam Fink:    I think what we believed was true when we started this business is still true for the most part. Right? Like, we've always believed in being open communicators. We've always believed internally in, you know, the power of learning from each other, the power of collaboration. I think those are all important things. We've always believed in wanting people who are excellent at their craft. When we started to think about it, it's that as a growing business, it's actually time to write that down for the first time and distill it into the things that matter most for us. And that is what led us to kind of starting to think more about culture and principles in the last few weeks than we had previously. Ned Koh:      To that point, a really interesting thing that we've been discussing, especially with some of the larger implications of being able to model behavior, is this idea of like trustworthiness of a model. There's a very big difference between being worthy of trust and being a trustworthy company. And we certainly try to stay on the prior, right? We define that as being worthy of trust to the people who work next to you, right? That you're going to do an incredible job. It's being worthy of trust of your investors. It's being worthy of trust of your customers. It's being worthy of trust of the world that you're using the technology for the biggest impacts you can. Ned Koh:      Thank you so much for having us, Marco. Marco Argenti:      Was great. And good luck. Thank you so much. title: GS Q3 Operating Profit Jumps 46% on Caltex Refining Margins - Seoul Economic Daily

Q3 operating profit reaches 1.3 trillion won
GS Caltex operating profit soars 208% from a year earlier
Revenue rises 11% to 7.3 trillion won
Profit falls from prior quarter on higher crude shipping rates GS Holdings (078930.KS) lifted its third-quarter operating profit 46% from a year earlier, helped by strong refining margins and a robust lubricants business. Profit fell from the previous quarter, however, as surging crude shipping rates and inventory-related losses from falling oil prices and a weaker won weighed on results. Third-quarter operating profit on a consolidated basis came to 1.2748 trillion won ($872 million), up 46.4% from the same period a year earlier, the company said on the 5th. Revenue rose 11.2% to 7.2706 trillion won and net profit climbed 66.9% to 680.4 billion won. Compared with the preceding quarter, operating profit fell 25.8% and net profit dropped 39.9%. GS Caltex, in which GS Holdings holds a 50% stake through intermediate holding company GS Energy, drove the improvement. Its third-quarter operating profit surged 208% from a year earlier to 1.1447 trillion won. Geopolitical risks, including disruptions at refineries worldwide, kept refining margins elevated, lifting operating profit at the refining division 183% to 696.8 billion won. In lubricants, supply disruptions kept base oil margins high, pushing operating profit up 221% to a record 448.9 billion won. Against the prior quarter, however, GS Caltex's operating profit fell 55%. The decline reflected a plunge in refining division operating profit to about one-third of the second quarter's 2.1993 trillion won. Crude procurement costs, including shipping and insurance, rose, and the company booked inventory-related losses as it refined and sold crude purchased at higher prices. The petrochemical division remained in the red with an operating loss of 1 billion won, though the shortfall narrowed from 6.3 billion won in the second quarter as aromatics margins improved following utilization adjustments for scheduled maintenance. Results at energy affiliates were mixed. GS EPS, a power generation subsidiary, saw operating profit slip 25% from a year earlier to 56.3 billion won after an individual tariff contract for its No. 1 liquefied natural gas unit expired and its No. 3 unit underwent maintenance. GS E&R posted a 2% rise in operating profit to 31.7 billion won on higher system marginal prices. GS Global (001250.KS), which builds offshore wind foundation structures through subsidiary GS Entec, reported a 39% drop in operating profit to 3.9 billion won amid related transition work. A GS official said uncertainty would persist in the fourth quarter from oil price volatility tied to conditions in the Middle East and from recently surging crude shipping rates, adding that how flexibly the company responds to shifting market conditions will determine future earnings. title: Sacha Baron Cohen On How Australia's COVID Lockdowns and a Fake Tour Led to Ali G's Comeback - Screen Realm
content: Sacha Baron Cohen has explained how Ali G’s comeback began with a stand-up tour that didn’t exist. During Australia’s COVID lockdowns, the comedian talked his way into Western Australia by promising jobs and a financial boost. Then a police inspector turned up expecting him to put on a show. That hastily assembled performance would ultimately inspire Ali G: Who Iz I?, the character’s first feature film since 2002’s Ali G Indahouse. Speaking on Deadline’s Comedy Means Business podcast, Baron Cohen recalled learning that Western Australia had far fewer restrictions than Sydney. His initial application to enter the state was rejected, but he discovered a potential loophole. “And then I find out you can get into Western Australia if you prove that there is financial benefit for Western Australia to have you in,” he explained. “And so I say, ‘Okay, I’m doing a standup tour and it’s going to create a hundred jobs…’ And the police say, ‘You’re in.'” It worked. He was granted entry and completed 14 days of quarantine. Unfortunately, the authorities hadn’t forgotten about the supposed tour. “At the end, a police car turns up and this inspector comes out and she says, ‘I’m in charge of your standup tour,'” he recalled. “Now, there was no stand-up tour. And so I had to do a standup show.” With a performance suddenly required, Baron Cohen put together an act featuring four characters: an ultra-left-wing persona, Brüno, Borat and Ali G. The audience responded enthusiastically to Brüno and Borat, but something rather strange happened when he brought out his tracksuit-wearing troublemaker from Staines. “When I started doing Ali G, it was a really weird response in the audience in that they treated him like he was a real person,” Baron Cohen said. “And the rest of them, they’re aware that it’s me, Sacha, doing Borat. They’re really excited. But Ali was somehow seen as a real person.” Baron Cohen had a theory about why Ali G, unlike his other characters, still seemed so convincing to the audience. “I think it was because he’s disappeared for 20 years,” he explained. “And the second reason, the more important one was before I came out as Sacha, I was Ali G. So I did no press. I did no interviews. There were no photos of me. Nobody knew what I looked like.” He even recalled standing in an HMV record shop dressed as Borat, surrounded by Ali G fans who had absolutely no idea who he was. All those years later, that old illusion apparently still had some life in it. The Perth audience’s reaction left him wondering: “Is there a movie in him?” Turns out there was. The result is Ali G: Who Iz I?, a secretly filmed mockumentary that also marks Baron Cohen’s feature directorial debut. It follows Ali G to America after he discovers that his girlfriend Julie (Morgana Robinson) is eight months pregnant. Unlike the largely scripted Ali G Indahouse, the new film brings back the comedian’s undercover approach, placing his characters alongside unsuspecting real people. Unfortunately, the movie’s release hasn’t exactly gone smoothly. Originally intended for a wide theatrical rollout, Ali G: Who Iz I? ended up with a dramatically reduced US cinema release before arriving on Prime Video on October 28, just five days after opening in theatres. Amazon MGM Studios subsequently extended some screenings, but it’s hardly the theatrical comeback one might have expected. The reviews haven’t been particularly encouraging, either. At the time of writing, the film holds just 38% on Rotten Tomatoes, with critics questioning whether Baron Cohen’s outrageous style of comedy still has the same impact. Not quite the triumphant return Baron Cohen might have hoped for. Baron Cohen is also once again declaring that he’s finished with the elaborate undercover comedy that made him famous. He reiterated that intention during the Deadline podcast, suggesting that Ali G: Who Iz I? will be his final film made in this style. He made similar comments in a recent Hollywood Reporter interview, describing the enormous challenges and risks involved in these productions. Between the complicated logistics, dangerous situations and death threats he’s faced over the years, the comedian insists he’s ready to move on. He’s also ruled out another Borat film. Of course, there’s reason to take the retirement announcement with a pinch of salt. Baron Cohen announced Ali G’s retirement back in 2007 and has repeatedly suggested his days of undercover stunts were behind him, including around the release of 2020’s Borat Subsequent Moviefilm. Yet here we are, with Ali G back in his tracksuit and another collection of unsuspecting participants caught up in the madness. ‘Finally’: Bobby Lee’s Long-Awaited First Stand-Up Special Gets Hulu Trailer Druski Announces Netflix Deal and ‘Collect & Praise’ Series: Trailer and Everything to Know

title: CU, BGF Retail drives first-ever quarterly operating profit above 100 billion won… GS Retail posts 'quarterly record' - 머니투데이
content:
CU drives BGF Retail's operating profit above 100 billion won for first time as GS Retail posts record quarterly earnings Driven by the growth momentum of convenience store CU, BGF Retail surpassed 100 billion won in quarterly operating profit for the first time in its history. The strong performance was underpinned by the success of differentiated products leveraging mega-hit intellectual property (IP) and an increase in sales to foreign customers. Competitor GS Retail posted its highest-ever quarterly operating profit, but convenience store GS25 saw a decline in operating profit due to the reflection of one-time costs related to merchandise. GS25 plans to restore profitability by strengthening store competitiveness and expanding differentiated products. BGF Retail announced on the 5th that its consolidated operating profit for the third quarter of this year reached 100.8 billion won, a 3.2% increase from the same period last year. This is the first time quarterly operating profit has exceeded 100 billion won. Revenue rose by 2.1% to 2.5152 trillion won compared to the same period last year. BGF Retail's strong results were driven by its core business, convenience store CU. Although BGF Retail reports its results on a consolidated basis that includes the performance of affiliates such as BGF Logistics, BGF Networks, and BGF Eco Materials, CU accounts for approximately 97% of revenue and operating profit. Effectively, CU's performance determines the overall results of BGF Retail. Despite unfavorable business conditions, including the base effect from last year's consumption coupon distribution and summer heatwaves, CU maintained its growth momentum thanks to increased sales to foreign customers and strong sales of processed foods. In particular, product launches and marketing leveraging popular IPs such as Rescene proved effective. Differentiated products, including coffee candy and truffle ham snacks, also contributed to revenue growth. The expansion of sales to foreigners also boosted performance growth. The increase in total store sales for the third quarter showed that 35.5% was attributable to increased sales to foreign customers. The share of foreigners in total revenue also rose from 1.5% in the same period last year to 2.5%. It is analyzed that strategies aimed at enhancing purchasing convenience for foreign customers, such as immediate tax refund services and the operation of unmanned currency exchange kiosks, were effective. BGF Retail plans to enhance profitability by expanding its IP-based differentiated product lines and strengthening efforts to attract foreign customers. Additionally, the company intends to secure a medium- to long-term profit foundation by maintaining an expansion policy focused on high-profitability stores and increasing the proportion of mid-to-large-sized stores ranging from 25 to 40 pyeong (approximately 83 to 132 square meters). GS Retail, which operates convenience store GS25, also recorded a quarterly operating profit of 132.1 billion won, its highest ever on a quarterly basis. Revenue increased by 3.4% from the same period last year to 3.3143 trillion won. GS Retail's strong results were driven by its supermarket and home shopping businesses. Supermarket GS The Fresh achieved record-high quarterly performance in both revenue and operating profit. Home shopping channel GS Shop also recorded an operating profit of 24.2 billion won, a 108.6% increase. However, GS25, which forms a duopoly structure in the convenience store market alongside CU, saw its performance slow down due to the impact of one-time costs related to merchandise. GS25's third-quarter operating profit was 78.2 billion won, an 8.1% decrease from the same period last year. GS25 explained that the decline in operating profit was not due to a structural deterioration in profitability. It stated that approximately 9.4 billion won in costs incurred during merchandise operations and transactions, including losses from inventory management, were reflected in the results. If these are simply excluded, operating profit would be 87.6 billion won, exceeding the performance of the same period last year. GS25 plans to accelerate its turnaround in the fourth quarter by strengthening store competitiveness and expanding differentiated products. The company intends to enhance store competitiveness through store enlargement, relocation to prime locations, and the expansion of stores focused on fresh food. Additionally, it aims to expand revenue through the development of differentiated products such as Minumsa Bread, targeting demand from foreign tourists, and expanding its quick commerce business. title: China's Buick Electra GS Is A Stylish Hybrid America Can't Have - CarScoops
content: GM could definitely use plug-in hybrid sedan in its U.S. lineup Buick hasn't offered a sedan in the U.S. since sales of the Regal ended in 2020. But it's a totally different story in China, where SUV haters can choose from multiple low-riding four-door cars, including the handsome, electrified Electra L7. Now, Buick's Chinese division is gearing up to launch its Electra GS little brother, and you have to wonder if America is missing out. Details of the Electra GS were revealed by China's Ministry of Industry and Information Technology filings ahead of the official debut, and they tell us the production car has changed quite a bit since GM showed the Electra GS concept (below) at the Shanghai Auto Show in 2025. The LED headlights have been inverted, and the Buick badge moved from the hood to a front facia that features less body-color plastic. The concept was incredibly handsome, but maybe looked a little too much like a Tesla Model 3 around the front. The production car looks less like a Tesla, but sacrifices some eye candy points. An imminent ban on pop-out door handles in China meant the concept's had to go, and though the fastback profile is carried across, the show car's traditional sedan trunk has made way for a more practical hatch. The taillights are also new, and so is the "Buick" lettering spelled out at the rear of the car. Another genuinely massive change is the productions GS's massive reduction in scale. MIIT data shows it's 196.1 inches (4,980 mm) long, but the concept (pictured above) was a huge 208.7 inches (5,300 mm). Same thing with wheelbase. The concept's axles were 126 inches (3,200 mm) apart, but the production GS wheelbase measures 112.8 inches (2,865 mm), making the finished car similar in size to a Toyota Crown, rather than a Mercedes S-Class. The biggest switch of all, though, takes place under the hood. GM didn't reveal much in the way of technical details about the concept, but it did confirm it was a fully electric car that rode on a dedicated EV platform, giving a totally flat floor. But, like Adam West's 1966 Batman jumping on the Batpoles inside Wayne Manor dressed in a comfy cardigan, and emerging inside the Batcave in full caped crusader garb 100 ft (31 m) down, the GS bound for dealers has arrived for duty as a plug-in hybrid. Base cars pair a 97 horsepower (98 PS) naturally aspirated 1.5-liter inline-4 with a 221 hp (224 PS) electric motor, but a more expensive variant swaps the NA gas motor for a turbocharged version of the same, making 154 hp (156 PS). We'll have wait for the full China debut to find out more about the GS, including whether the interior looks anything like the concept's (below). But don't pin your hopes on seeing that yoke steering wheel — we can already see a conventional steering wheel is present in the studio images of the exterior. Back in the U.S., GM's sales have been hurt by its lack of hybrid offerings. The automaker was so sure EVs would dominate the car market by the end of the decade that it didn't bother developing them, except for the Corvette E-Ray (now renamed Grand Sport X). Rival brands like Toyota and Hyundai hedged their bets, and made both, and are now reaping the rewards, while GM is rushing to catch up toward the end of the decade. Could the GS work here? Absolutely, but it's not likely. GM does import vehicles from China, including Chinese-built Buick Envision from China, although production of that model is due to shift to Kansas in 2028. Complicating matters is the fact that the GS is the result of a joint venture between GM and China's SAIC, and new restrictions on Chinese software that take effect with the 2027 model year would make it tricky to get this car compliant for the U.S. market, even if production was shifted to North America to avoid tariffs. Overall, we'd say don't hold your breath for this Buick.

title: Crazy Like Jeremy Fox: Birdie G’s Returns While The Restaurant at Edna Marks a New Chapter - Observer
content: What is it like to open two high-profile restaurants, in two different cities, in less than two weeks? For chef Jeremy Fox, it’s a crazy but surprisingly calming experience. You can opt out anytime. Fox, a versatile chef who followed up his “On Vegetables” cookbook with his “On Meat” cookbook, has worked in the top tier of fine dining in California and also created comforting, nostalgic food that celebrates Americana and the Jewish-American diaspora. In Los Angeles, he’s long been a leader of seasonal, market-driven cuisine. But recently, it was unclear whether he would cook in a restaurant again. He closed Birdie G’s, a deeply personal restaurant named for his daughter and inspired by his grandmother’s home cooking, in Santa Monica at the end of 2025. The closure, one of many in L.A. spurred by an economic downturn, left Fox unmoored. But now Birdie G’s is back, with an expanded repertoire, at a high-profile new location in Los Angeles. On October 26, Fox opened the new Birdie G’s inside the Fairmont Century Plaza hotel. Unlike the previous dinner-only Birdie G’s, the new restaurant serves breakfast, lunch and dinner. “It’s a muscle I’ve never used before,” Fox told Observer on opening night after we ate his fried-oyster-topped riff on Caesar salad, soul-warming matzo ball soup, “pickle chick” schnitzel and Flannery steak frites before indulging in a slice of jiggly rose petal pie. What added to the craziness is that Fox knew he would be in San Luis Obispo a few days later for friends-and-family service at The Restaurant at Edna. Fox and former Birdie G’s executive chef Matthew Schaler will open that vineyard restaurant, with a focus on local agriculture, on Thursday, November 5. The timing of restaurant openings is always unpredictable, and the original goal was to open Birdie G’s and The Restaurant at Edna months apart. “I will say that I planned to open both restaurants in the same week,” Fox joked this week when Observer asked him about his intense timeline. “That was the goal. I nailed it.” But the reality is, he is now the opposite of unmoored, and it’s a good feeling. “I’ve made no attempts to hide that I deal with anxiety,” Fox, who’s known for speaking freely about his mental health, tells Observer. “I spent much of this year pretty deep in anxiety because I didn’t have a place to go every day. I was used to having deadlines every day. I had to be ready for service every day. And my deadlines were all, like, eight months away. It was an anxiety of, like, ‘Am I achieving as much in my day as I should?’ … But as things ramped up in the last two-and-a-half months, I’ve actually been calmer. I’ve always been someone who, the more engaged I am, the more semi-overwhelmed I am, the calmer I am, and the more I’m able to block out the noise. As it’s gotten crazier, I’ve gotten calmer.” It helps, of course, that he’s got an arsenal of dishes and techniques that he’s honed for decades. At Birdie G’s, he’s put a Rancho Gordo yellow eye bean stew on the lunch menu. That stew originated at Manresa, when David Kinch asked Fox to help create a patio menu. Fox then served the stew at Ubuntu and Rustic Canyon. The stew “appears to have an ungodly amount of garlic,” Fox says. “The garlic has to be cooked a certain amount, or else it disappears or overpowers the stew. It’s a matter of toasting the rosemary, the chili flakes and the garlic and olive oil, but not to the point where the garlic takes on any color. But it does have to be cooked through.” Meanwhile, making Birdie G’s matzo ball soup, which is enriched with carrot miso, is a “regimented” process. Fox was influenced by both how his grandmother Gladys made matzo ball soup and how specific his wife, Rachael Sheridan, is about chicken broth when she makes matzo ball soup. Birdie G’s is about Fox’s family and his desire to make everyday food. The Restaurant at Edna, with its focus on seasonal cooking and regional wines, is about using a different kind of muscle, one that Fox has called upon a lot in his career. “It’s designed for the things I’m good at,” Fox says of the dinner-only, five-night-a-week restaurant. “There’s no concept to it. This is one of the ways I like to cook, where the menu changes constantly. It’s based on the buildability of the best local ingredients, prepared thoughtfully. Not fussy, though. The room begs itself to be a destination restaurant, but we really want to try to not fall into that. We want to be someplace where you can go every week, and there will be new things on the menu as well as things you remember that you had last time. And then dishes might be gone forever, or they might come back next year.” During friends-and-family dinners, Fox and Schaler got raves for dishes like cone cabbage stuffed with smoked bacon, ramps and an egg-yolk sauce; sweet potato and pumpkin pavé with brown butter sabayon, sage and truffles; and mushroom ravioli shaped like mushrooms and featuring fonduta made with Stepladder Moonstone cheese. There’s also the Edna salad, with a beet-based French dressing that Schaler impressed Fox with when he was applying to work at the original Birdie G’s. The Restaurant at Edna will serve local seafood like Petrale sole and California meat like Flannery beef. Fox is buying ingredients from nearby farms that previously supplied him in Los Angeles for more than a decade. He’s looking at shellfish from uni diver Stephanie Mutz. This is his wheelhouse. But life, as Fox has long known, is about different things being true at the same time. Fox and his family eat at Silver Lake’s Astro diner more than any other restaurant in Los Angeles. He very much wants Birdie G’s to be a comforting, unintimidating, everyday L.A. restaurant. “The restaurants that originally inspired me to want to be part of the restaurant business were Applebee’s, Chili’s, The Cheesecake Factory, those kinds of places,” Fox says. “I went to culinary school and followed the path of fine dining when, originally, all I wanted to do was have a place that people like to go eat.” “It’s accessible food,” he says. “It’s recognizable. The original Birdie G’s was a crowd-pleaser. People who came really loved it and connected with it. A lot of people would say they haven’t had anything like that since their grandmother cooked it.” But most grandmothers don’t do things like make a Caesar salad enhanced by “A.C.G.” powder with anchovies, capers and garlic that are cooked down in olive oil for more than a day and then strained and dehydrated. Fox thinks a lot about the two dramatically contrasting restaurants in the movie “Big Night” and how he finds them both compelling. “Birdie G’s, for me, was a way to kind of have one foot in both worlds, with the understated subtle cuisine and also the more over-the-top and accessible food while trying to be a little bit subversive,” he says. The food at Birdie G’s is delicious and fun and a little crazy. For Fox, there’s comfort in the craziness. We get it: you like to have control of your own internet experience. title: Text of Pope Leo's Nov. 4 general audience - Catholic Standard
content: The following is the full text of Pope Leo XIV’s general audience address given Nov. 4 at St. Peter’s Square. The Documents of the Second Vatican Council. IV. Constitution Gaudium et Spes. 8. Faith and social, political, and economic life Dear brothers and sisters, good morning and welcome! The social dimension is an integral part not only of human nature, but also of our faith in Christ Jesus, as the precious legacy we receive from the Incarnation of the Son of God. The Constitution Gaudium et Spes (GS) recalls this in Chapters III and IV of Part II, dedicated to economic and social life and to the life of the political community. In these areas too, the Christian faith offers criteria for discernment. The Council Fathers highlight, first of all, the threat to world peace deriving from the imbalances linked to an economic development that is neither equitable nor respectful of creation (cf. GS, 63). This is a far-sighted vision, which was unfortunately borne out towards the end of the last century and which we see even more clearly today. To correct this course, the Document warns, technical progress alone is not enough: “many reforms in the socioeconomic realm and a change of mentality and attitude are required of all” (ibid.). Therefore, Gaudium et Spes summarizes the Christian vision of economic development, which must always be at the service of humankind and under human control (cf. GS, 64–65). The concept of integral development is already clearly evident here, a concept which Saint Paul VI would later place at the heart of his Encyclical Populorum Progressio (1967). More relevant than ever are the appeals to commit to eliminating discrimination against the most vulnerable social groups and migrants (cf. GS, 66). The heart of the economy is work. Through it, one develops as a person, provides for family needs, expresses one’s own talent, participates in social life and builds a better world by collaborating in God’s creative work. Work must never be distorted to the detriment of people, the common good or creation. The real challenge is to offer everyone opportunities to make the most of their abilities: unemployment, exploitation and working conditions that endanger health and life itself are unacceptable (cf. GS, 67). Workers have the right and the duty to participate in decisions affecting their work, including through trade unions, resolving conflicts through dialogue and non-violent action (cf. GS, 68). In this context, the Council recalls one of the fundamental principles of social teaching, namely the universal destination of earthly goods (cf. GS, 69) and applies it to the financial sphere, stating that “whoever makes decisions concerning these investments and the planning of the economy – whether they be individuals or groups of public authorities – are bound … to recognize their serious obligation of watching, on the one hand, that provision be made for the necessities required for a decent life both of individuals and of the whole community and, on the other, of looking out for the future and of establishing a right balance between the needs of present-day consumption, both individual and collective, and the demands of investing for the generation to come” (GS, 70). Gaudium et Spes then goes on to discuss the political community, noting several positive developments in the contemporary era, above all the fact that “the present keener sense of human dignity has given rise in many parts of the world to attempts to bring about a politico-juridical order which will give better protection to the rights of the person in public life” (GS, 73). The political community exists for the sake of the common good, which consists of “the sum of those conditions of the social life whereby men, families and associations more adequately and readily may attain their own perfection” (GS, 74). The exercise of political authority must always be directed towards the common good, which must be structured and operate according to local and historical circumstances, but always with the good of the entire human family at heart (cf. ibid.). Gaudium et Spes reiterates that “the Church and the political community in their own fields are autonomous and independent from each other. Yet both, under different titles, are devoted to the personal and social vocation of the same men. The more that both foster sounder cooperation between themselves with due consideration for the circumstances of time and place, the more effective will their service be exercised for the good of all” (GS, 76). Dear friends, engaging in economic and political life in accordance with these criteria is a way of building peace. As Pope Francis recalled, “war is a failure of politics and of humanity, a shameful capitulation, a stinging defeat before the forces of evil” (Encyclical Letter Fratelli tutti, 261). On the contrary, politics that tends to the wounds of peoples and of those who suffer injustice offers grounds for hope for the future of humanity. For this reason, I encourage young people to follow the example of those men and women who have borne faithful witness in these fields. And I renew my call to Christian communities to revive formation in the social doctrine of the Church. I greet all the English-speaking pilgrims and visitors taking part in today’s Audience, especially those from England, Ireland, Denmark, Malta, the Netherlands, Norway, Nigeria, Australia, Indonesia, Japan, the Philippines, Thailand, Vietnam and the United States of America. In a particular way, I welcome the members of the National Conference of Vocation Directors for England and Wales. Upon all of you and your families, I invoke the joy and peace of our Lord Jesus Christ. God bless you! Pope Leo XIV smiles from the popemobile while riding around St. Peter’s Square at the Vatican before his weekly general audience Nov. 4, 2026. (CNS photo/Lola Gomez)

Just two weeks into the NBA season, storylines have been flipped as injuries and surprise surges reverberate around the league. The Philadelphia 76ers have dominated their opponents early -- and are having some fun in the process. Meanwhile, the reigning champion New York Knicks are attempting to claw themselves back into the top echelon after starting the season 0-3. It's in the West where things have started to heat up. The Oklahoma City Thunder and Minnesota Timberwolves are dealing with injuries to their stars, making way for players such as the Memphis Grizzlies' Ty Jerome to have an early impact in his team's standings. The Los Angeles Lakers' Luka Doncic is making an early MVP case and doesn't seem to be slowing down after scoring 42 and 45 points in his past two games. And the Portland Trail Blazers, sans Ja Morant as he deals with an injury, are showing that depth is what will set teams apart across the league. In our second iteration of Power Rankings since the season started, our NBA insiders assigned four words to describe each team's start to 2026-27, and break down why things are -- or are not -- working. title: General Motors taps PHEV sedan segment with Buick Electra GS - CarNewsChina.com
content: General Motors is ready to launch the Buick Electra GS plug-in hybrid sedan in China. Built jointly with SAIC, it will compete with some high-volume models from BYD and Geely. The Electra GS is on time, as Buick’s deliveries declined by 20.4% Year-Over-Year in China, according to China EV DataTracker. The Buick Electra GS was exposed in China by the local Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT) during the domestic homologation process. It is a large sedan with dimensions of 4979/1914/1495 mm and a wheelbase of 2,865 mm. For clarity, it is 149 mm longer than the BYD Qin L DM-i sedan, marketed in some overseas markets under the Seal 6 name. The car’s exterior styling adopts a closed front end with a sizeable trapeze-shaped air intake, U-shaped headlights, semi-hidden door handles, a sleek roofline, a single taillight unit, and a ducktail spoiler. This sedan has approach and departure angles of 13 and 14 degrees, respectively. It rides on 18- or 19-inch wheels (225/50 R18 or 234/45 R19). The Electra GS can be optionally equipped with a roof-mounted LiDAR sensor. The curb weight lies between 1,780 and 1,890 kg. Its gross weight reaches 2,300 kg. The entry-level Buick Electra GS sedan comes standard with a 1.5-liter naturally aspirated 15FMC petrol-powered engine with a peak power output of 72 kW (97 hp). This ICE is manufactured by SAIC. The same ICE is used by the Roewe Jiayue 07 crossover, the Saic H5 (Shangjie H5), the Buick Electra E7 SUV, and other models. This engine is paired with a 165 kW (221 hp) electric motor. The car’s top speed is 190 km/h. It adopts two LFP battery pack variants from Zenergy and Rept Battero. A more powerful variant of the Buick Electra GS has a 1.5-liter turbocharged LD3 engine with a peak power output of 115 kW (154 hp). The same engine is used by the Buick Electra L7 sedan, the Buick GL8 PHEV minivan, and other cars. This ICE also works in pairs with a 165 kW (221 hp) electric motor. The top-trim Electra GS has a top speed of 190 km/h and a Zenergy-made LFP battery. It seems that the entry-level Buick Electra GS sedan will rival the mentioned BYD Qin L DM-i sedan. The latter model offers a combination of a 1.5-liter engine for 74 kW (99 hp) and an electric motor with a peak power output of 160 kW (215 hp). BYD delivered 70,740 units of this sedan to customers in China from January to September 2026, according to China EV DataTracker. The Electra GS is expected to cost more than 100,000 yuan (14,970 USD) domestically.

title: Buick Electra GS appears in China regulatory filing, expanding NEV lineup - CnEVPost
content: Buick's Electra GS plug-in hybrid sedan has appeared in China's latest regulatory filing catalog, revealing the fastback model's exterior and key powertrain specifications. China's Ministry of Industry and Information Technology released its 413th batch of new vehicle filings on Tuesday, with public comments open from November 4 to 10. The Electra GS has 3 variants in the filings, all manufactured by SAIC-GM, covering 2 engine options and different battery cell suppliers. Buick is a brand under General Motors (NYSE: GM). All 3 variants feature an electric motor with a peak output of 165 kW (221 hp). Their engines each have a displacement of 1,498 milliliters, with rated outputs of 72 kW for 2 variants and 115 kW for the remaining variant. All 3 variants use lithium iron phosphate batteries. One uses cells supplied by Rept Battero Energy (HKEX: 666), while the other 2 use cells from Zenergy. Battery packs for all variants are produced by a SAIC-GM subsidiary. The filings do not list battery capacity or electric range. Filing images show the Electra GS with a coupe-like fastback profile, slim headlights, a full-width taillight and semi-hidden door handles, along with Electra GS badging at the rear. The 5-seat sedan measures 4,979 mm in length and 1,914 mm in width, with a wheelbase of 2,865 mm. Height varies slightly across the filed variants. The images show roof-mounted LiDAR, while the filings also list an option without LiDAR, alongside choices of rear spoilers, brake calipers and exterior trim. The filings do not disclose the supplier or specific capabilities of the driver-assistance system, nor do they detail final trim levels, pricing or launch timing. The Electra GS filing comes as Buick continues to update its new energy vehicle (NEV) lineup in China. On September 23, the brand launched an updated Electra E7 plug-in hybrid SUV, just 5 months after its initial launch. The Electra E7 update focused on powertrain and driver-assistance equipment, with the Pro trim combining a 1.5-liter turbocharged engine and advanced driver-assistance features. title: Former CEO of SGX-listed GS Holdings charged over false trading - The Business Times
content: Now known as Octopus (Apac) Holdings, the company has expanded into beverage distribution [SINGAPORE] The former CEO of GS Holdings, Pang Pok, was charged in court on Wednesday (Nov 4) with abetting a conspiracy to engage in share price manipulation and perverting the course of justice, said the Singapore Police Force. title: The Best Lexus GS Isn't The Inline-Six, It's The 300-HP V8 - HotCars
content: Eric Tipan has spent more than 30 years working across journalism, broadcasting and live media. He’s a five-time Henry Ford Award winner, has covered the Olympic Games for TV5 and One Sports, called international volleyball for Volleyball World, and written and presented automotive stories for AutoIndustriya.com and Manila Bulletin. Before that, radio was a big part of his career. Nearly 25 years of it, as a presenter, program director and production lead. That range shows up in the way he works. Whether he’s writing, editing or speaking live on air, Eric has a knack for making technical or fast-moving subjects easier to understand without stripping away the detail that makes them interesting. Most luxury sedans don't look like they could hit 60 mph in 5.8 seconds, clear the quarter-mile in 14.5 seconds, and reach an electronically limited 149 mph on a track. Lexus recorded those figures with prototypes of the 300-hp V8 version of the second-generation Lexus GS. Not bad for a car dressed for a board meeting. Yet buyers often chase its Supra-related inline-six, which made 225 hp, or mistake it for the V6-powered ES 300. The engine with the bigger reputation might not be the better used-car buy. Under the GS 300's hood, six pistons rise and fall in one long row, with 24 valves controlling how the engine breathes. This 3.0-liter 2JZ-GE made 225 hp and 220 lb-ft in 1998, driving the rear wheels through an automatic. But the Supra family connection doesn't include the turbocharged Supra's hardware, and chasing that extra power means building a turbo car, not unlocking a factory secret. There's another trap under the Lexus badge. The ES 300's 1MZ-FE is a V6 mounted sideways for front-wheel drive. The GS 300 has a straight-six stretching lengthwise, with power going rearward. Open their hoods and the layout tells two different stories. Even service access changes; an ES repair complaint isn't evidence against the GS.In Japan, the second-generation Lexus GS was sold as the Toyota Aristo. The Aristo S300 used the same naturally aspirated 2JZ-GE as the U.S. GS 300, while the V300 packed a twin-turbo 2JZ-GTE rated at 280 PS (about 276 hp). The JZX100 Chaser Tourer V was a different car altogether, running a turbocharged 2.5-liter 1JZ-GTE. The 1998–2000 Lexus GS 400 hid serious speed behind familiar sheet metal. Its 4.0-liter 1UZ-FE V8 pumps out 300 hp and 310 lb-ft, an extra 75 hp and 90 lb-ft over the GS 300. Lexus's factory specifications put prototype 0–60 mph acceleration at 5.8 seconds, versus 7.6 for the six-cylinder. You get that speed without opening a turbo catalog. The four-cam V8 combines aluminum construction with variable valve timing to manage how its cylinders breathe. The GS 400 weighs just 55 pounds more than its six-cylinder sibling. A five-speed automatic feeds the rear wheels, while double-wishbone suspension guides them through bumps and corners. Steering-wheel E-shift buttons let you choose gears without reaching for the console. Traction control helps tame wheelspin. It's still an automatic, but Lexus gave the driver more to work with than a plain selector. The 2001 GS 430 trades 4.0 liters for 4.3 and brings 325 lb-ft at 3,400 rpm instead of the older V8's 310 at 4,000. Both make 300 hp; Lexus claimed the same 5.8-second run. If that car is better maintained, its extra torque makes it worth considering. A 300-hp Lexus V8 for $7,600? That's enough to make you check the listing twice. A 1998 GS 400 with 149,000 miles sold for that price on Bring a Trailer on June 22, 2026. Another '98, showing 48,000 miles, sold there for $12,000 on May 17. That's $4,400 extra for 101,000 fewer miles. Then inspect both. The cheaper car disclosed oil-pan and steering-rack leaks, plus a patch covering worn driver's-seat upholstery. The low-mileage one had a replacement instrument cluster calibrated to the removed unit's mileage and a faded dashboard beneath a pad. Neither was frozen in a showroom time capsule. Those winning bids also exclude buyer fees and taxes, and they aren't a market average or a guaranteed price range. Repairs can make a used Lexus bargain less charming. JDMBUYSELL reported a $15,950 Aristo median from 37 seller-reported sales dated August 2023 through October 2026, as of November 1, 2026. But those cars span generations and specifications. It's not proof of a fixed JDM premium over a GS 400. Compare cars, including fees and repairs. The GS 400 serves up luxury and muscle on the same plate: leather seats, walnut trim, dual-zone climate control, and a 300-hp V8. Before you fall for it, though, check dated receipts and mileage. Gates lists a timing-belt replacement interval of 90,000 miles or 72 months, whichever comes first. On this interference V8, a failed belt can mean pistons meeting valves, and nobody wants that introduction. Have a specialist review the belt-driven water pump, too. The S160's hydraulic brake booster, pump, accumulator, and ABS require model-specific pressure and electrical checks; warning lights or odd pump behavior deserve a repair estimate. Check stored faults, leaks, suspension wear, and the dashboard under any cover. Fading on one auction car doesn't make later-generation sticky-dashboard bulletins an S160 diagnosis. With proper maintenance and a clean inspection, this GS 400 makes a compelling used luxury sedan. But if repairs swallow the bargain, walk away. You came for a 300-hp Lexus, not a restoration project. Sources: Lexus, Toyota, Bring a Trailer, JDMBUYSELL, Gates We want to hear from you. title: GS Shop adopts AWS-built AI to speed promotion planning by 70% in Korea - Chosunbiz
content: Ai-driven system co-built with AWS helps GS Shop MDs quickly curate products, map stores, and craft event themes GS Shop will use artificial intelligence (AI) to streamline merchandise planners' (MDs') promotion prep work. GS Shop said on the 3rd it has officially adopted the "MD curation system," co-developed with Amazon Web Services (AWS). When an MD enters the intent and conditions for a promotion plan, AI analyzes sales performance and customer behavior data to select suitable products and supports everything from building the promotion to registration. According to GS Shop, MDs in charge of product operations in the mobile application (app) have spent about 40% of their total work hours on promotion prep. That is because they have had to perform repetitive tasks such as checking product information and sales performance, and selecting and arranging products to participate in events. The newly introduced system consists of four AI agents: product curation, automatic store mapping, trend sensing, and copywriting. AI narrows down up to 1,000 candidate products based on sales performance and customer data and recommends products that fit the planning intent. MDs can enter desired conditions into the AI to filter products. After product selection, AI classifies and arranges products by type. It also analyzes internal and external data to recommend event themes and suggest event names and marketing copy. In a pilot run over the past month, about 40% of all promotions were created through the system. The time required for product selection and event prep fell by about 70% from before. During the pilot, 72% of mobile MDs used the system, and GS Shop plans to raise the usage rate to over 90% within the year. Kim Yohan, head of the home shopping AX division at GS Retail, said, "By collaborating with the AWS Generative AI Innovation Center, we were able to strengthen field-centric AX (AI transformation) capabilities," and added, "We will continue to spread a work culture in which practitioners and developers find solutions with AI and lead to practical business consolidation."
